title: Demoing HR software when HR, IT and finance all sit in the same evaluation
summary: How to demo HR software when HR, IT and finance all judge it. Storylane data on demo length and buying committees, plus a three-path demo plan.
body_markdown:
Watch a live demo of HR software and you can usually tell who is in the room. If the HR leader is there, the demo spends twenty minutes on the employee experience: the onboarding checklist, the self-service portal, the manager approving time off from a phone. Then the deal moves on, and two people who were never on the call open the recording. Someone from IT wants to know how the system talks to everything else and who can see salary data. Someone in finance wants to know what it costs and whether payroll will still come out right. Neither of them sat through the part they cared about, because there was no such part.


I think this is the central problem in demoing HR software. One product, three buyers, and each one judges it on a different question. My answer is what I call **the three-path demo** : build the demo as three short paths, one each for HR, IT and finance, instead of one long tour that tries to satisfy all of them and ends up serving whoever showed up.


## Why is demoing HR software harder than demoing most software?


Most B2B products have one natural owner. A sales tool belongs to sales, a marketing tool to marketing. HR software touches every employee, holds the most sensitive personal data a company keeps, and sits next to payroll. So three functions get a real say, and they rarely agree on what matters.


Buyer The question they bring What they need to see


HR (the champion, usually) Will employees and managers actually use this? The everyday flows: onboarding, self-service, approvals, from the employee's and the manager's point of view


IT and security Will this fit our stack, and who can see what? Integrations with the systems they already run, single sign-on, user roles and permissions, where employee data lives


Finance What will this cost us, and will the numbers be right? Payroll accuracy, reporting, how cost changes with headcount


The table is my view of the typical split, not a dataset. The point it makes is simple: these are three different demos. The HR demo is about feel. The IT demo is about plumbing. The finance demo is about trust in the numbers. A single click path cannot be all three without becoming long.


## Most of the HR software buying committee never sees your live demo


The obvious fix is to get all three on the call. In practice that rarely happens, and our own data shows why. In an analysis of[637 mid-market and enterprise deals and 2,021 recorded sales conversations](https://www.storylane.io/blog/what-637-b2b-deals-taught-us-about-buying-committees) , the average buying account had about 23 known contacts in the CRM (median 10), while the average call had 2.3 people on it. Roughly one in five known contacts ever joined a call. Of 6,187 people invited to calls, 4,547 turned up, about 73%.


That dataset covers B2B software in general, not HR tech alone, so treat it as the base rate rather than an HR-specific number. But the pattern fits HR deals well. The HR leader takes the calls because they are the one who feels the pain. IT and finance weigh in later, through a forwarded recording, a security review or a budget meeting your team never attends.


So the real question is not "how do I get IT and finance into the demo?" It is "what does each of them see when the champion forwards it?"


## Why one long demo loses all three buyers


Here is the mechanism as I understand it. Every buyer adds a detour to a shared demo. Add the integrations section for IT and the HR leader waits through ten screens of settings. Add the payroll reporting for finance and IT waits through it too. Each detour serves one person and costs the other two. The demo gets longer, and length has a price.


We measured that price once. In our[analysis of demo lengths across 9 industries](https://www.storylane.io/blog/learnings-from-analyzing-demo-lengths-across-9-industries) (34 marketing demos and 5,409 sessions, HR tech among them; a small sample, so read it as a direction rather than a law), longer demos had lower completion rates. The top 10% of demos were completed 64% of the time with an average of 9 steps. The bottom 10% were completed 1.39% of the time with an average of 37 steps. The overall average was 21 steps and 26% completion, and the study recommended 8 to 12 steps for marketing demos.


Two caveats matter. Those were website demos that buyers clicked through on their own, not live calls. And HR tech was neither among the shortest demos (product, marketing and sales tools) nor among the longest (cloud, security and data tools). But a forwarded demo is exactly a demo the buyer clicks through on their own. When your champion sends the recording or the link to IT, IT is in the same position as a website visitor: alone, busy and free to close the tab.


The same study had a line I keep coming back to. When a product cannot fit into a dozen steps, split it into flows and let people choose their own path. That is the three-path demo in one sentence.


## What should a good HR software demo include?


Three short paths and one shared opening. This is how I would build it.


### The shared opening (two or three steps)


One screen that states what the product does for this company, using their own job titles and headcount if you know them. Then a choice: "I'm in HR", "I'm in IT", "I'm in finance". The shared part should be short enough that nobody feels they are waiting for their bit.


### The HR path: one employee, start to finish


Follow one new hire from offer accepted to first day, then show one manager approving one request. Keep it to the moments an HR leader can picture their own people doing. Skip the admin settings. HR will configure the product later; right now they are deciding whether employees will use it.


### The IT path: how it connects and who sees what


Show the integrations with the kinds of systems IT already runs, single sign-on, and the permissions screen where you decide who can see salary and personal data. IT is not judging the interface. They are judging how much work and risk this adds to their week. If you have a security pack, this is where to point to it; our[security questionnaire playbook for presales](https://www.storylane.io/blog/security-questionnaire-presales) covers how to answer those reviews without stalling the deal.


### The finance path: the numbers they will sign off on


Show a payroll run and the report finance will read after it, then how cost moves as headcount grows. Finance wants to trust that the numbers come out right. One clear report beats a tour of every dashboard.


Each path should be short enough to finish in a few minutes. If a path is drifting past a dozen steps, it is probably two paths.


## What about the live call?


The strongest objection to all this comes from sales engineers, and it is a fair one. A good live demo is a conversation. You run discovery, you hear what this buyer cares about, and you adapt. A prebuilt path feels like a step backwards.


I agree about the call. Keep it live and keep it tailored. The three-path demo is not a replacement for the call. It is for the people who will never be on it, which by our own numbers is most of the committee. It also helps the call itself: if the HR leader already knows the IT path exists, you can spend the meeting on what they care about and stop squeezing in integrations "just in case IT asks".


There is a second objection: building three paths per deal sounds like a lot of work for a presales team that is already short of time. It is, if you build them from scratch for every deal. The better approach is to build the three paths once as a library and adjust the opening per account. If[demo environments are already your bottleneck](https://www.storylane.io/blog/sales-engineer-demo-environment-bottleneck) , prebuilt paths reduce the load rather than adding to it.


## What this looks like at a large HR tech company


Phenom, an HR tech company whose platform helps organisations hire, develop and retain people, is a useful example.[Phenom built 35 interactive demos in 3 weeks](https://www.storylane.io/customer-stories/how-phenom-built-35-demos-in-3-weeks-for-its-flagship-tradeshow) for its annual conference. Its product marketing team worked with product leaders, solutions consultants and knowledge management teams, and arranged the demos as 12 booths in a "pick your own adventure" lab, so HR leaders could choose their own route through the platform.


That is the same idea at event scale: many short paths instead of one long tour, and the visitor picks the one that matches their question. Phenom's team also took the demos beyond the event. Its sales teams now follow up customer calls with personalised demos. Their product marketer's advice to other demo builders was to write out the click path in advance and to keep the audience in mind. Both are exactly what a three-path demo forces you to do.


## What to do on Monday


Take your current HR software demo and mark every step with H, I or F: which of the three buyers is it for? You will probably find a long run of H steps, a few I steps squeezed in near the end, and almost nothing for F. That map is your first draft of three paths. Cut each one to a dozen steps or fewer, add a short shared opening, and give it to your next champion before they ask. The demo that wins an HR software deal is often the one IT and finance watched without you, so build that one on purpose. For more on reaching the people who skip the call, see our guide to[sales multithreading](https://www.storylane.io/blog/sales-multithreading) .
